items.value: Increased social sector spending is imperative for large-scale job creation
items.reasoning: The passage sets up a 24-million job gap, says e-commerce can close at best half of it, and then names what closes the other half: 'only those sectors that drive domestic demand such as health and education'. Health and education are the social sector, so expanding them is the passage's implied route to large-scale job creation. C is directly contradicted - the passage says services are not generating the additional jobs needed. A is never raised; the passage describes labour leaving agriculture without objecting to it. B picks up the aside that construction and unregistered manufacturing are 'not markedly better jobs', but that is a description of the problem, not the passage's implication about how to create jobs.

items.value: Assumptions 1 and 2 are valid - the State needs institutions to play its role in a digital society, and it must stop private parties from violating privacy
items.reasoning: The passage's concluding claim is that the State's role is 'not just to abstain' but 'to actively ensure that private parties are not able to block' a right, which applied to the passage's own subject - the right to privacy in the digital age - is exactly assumption 2. Assumption 1 is the enabling premise behind that same claim: a State that must actively guarantee rights in a digital society is presupposed to have the machinery to do so. Assumption 3 is not supported anywhere - the passage never says the digital economy and privacy are incompatible, only that rights need active protection. Assumption 1 is the judgement call, since the passage never uses the word 'institutions'; but it is the only reading on which the State's prescribed active role is achievable, and 3 is the clear distractor.

items.value: Wetlands need to be reinforced as more than just open sources of water
items.reasoning: The passage's complaint is that water is treated as a resource divorced from the rivers and wetlands it comes from, and that policy does not grasp that water is part of a natural ecosystem. The inference is therefore that wetlands must be valued and strengthened as ecological systems, not merely as taps - which is C. B is the opposite of the passage's point, since it criticises engineering efforts precisely for augmenting supply instead of strengthening ecological capacity. A introduces the Ramsar Convention, which the passage never mentions, and D introduces pricing, which it never discusses.

items.value: Spread your wealth across different kinds of assets so that risk is minimised
items.reasoning: The passage opens by calling asset allocation the most important investment decision, then argues that no asset is risk-free - even idle money - but that all the extreme risks will not manifest at the same time. That last point is precisely the argument for spreading money across asset classes, which is A. D states only the premise (investing is risky) and misses the suggestion built on it. B recommends a personality trait the passage never endorses, and C brings in professional asset managers, who are not mentioned at all.

items.value: Only assumptions 1 and 3 are valid - biotechnology regulation is an evolving process and must weigh socio-economic aspects
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 follows from the opening move: because multi-trait crops will be the norm in future, regulation 'cannot be understood solely in the context of the current generation of GM crops' - that is, regulation has to evolve with the technology. Assumption 3 is stated almost verbatim: the passage calls for a comprehensive look 'taking into account various aspects, including socio-economic impacts'. Assumption 2 fails because public participation in policy decisions is never mentioned. Assumption 4 fails because the passage links domestic regulation to trade policy and international treaties without saying anything about involving the political executive.

items.value: Biotechnology's role is not confined to the current priorities of developing GM crops
items.reasoning: The passage's pivot sentence is that biotechnology's role in agriculture and its regulation 'cannot be understood solely in the context of the current generation of GM crops', which C restates. B is wrong because the passage says not using biotechnology in the climate change action plan cannot be an option - an argument for using it, not a claim that it is currently unused. A introduces the precautionary principle, which never appears. D inverts the passage, which speaks of minimising negative impacts rather than claiming they are not understood.

items.value: 10 zeroes
items.reasoning: A trailing zero needs a pair of 2 and 5, so count each prime in the product. The factors of 5 come to 14 (one each from 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 35, 40, 45, 55, 60 and two each from 25 and 50), but the factors of 2 come to only 10 (one from 10, two from 20, one from 30, three from 40, one from 50, two from 60). The number of zeroes is the smaller count, 10. Computing the product directly gives 116943750000000000, which ends in exactly 10 zeroes. The trap is counting only the fives and answering 14.

items.value: It is not divisible by 9
items.reasoning: XYZ + YZX + ZXY = (100X+10Y+Z) + (100Y+10Z+X) + (100Z+10X+Y) = 111(X+Y+Z) = 3 x 37 x (X+Y+Z). So it is always divisible by 3, by 37 and by (X+Y+Z), ruling out A, C and D. The single factor of 3 comes from the 111; since the question stipulates that X+Y+Z is not a multiple of 3, no second factor of 3 is available, so the sum is never divisible by 9. Checking all 600 three-digit cases with a non-multiple-of-3 digit sum confirms the sum fails divisibility by 9 in every one and by 3, 37 and (X+Y+Z) in none.

items.value: r is the largest
items.reasoning: Set the common value to k. Then p = k + 2016, q = k - 2017, r = k + 2018 and s = k - 2019. Both q and s are below k, while p and r are above it, and r exceeds p because 2018 is greater than 2016. So r is the largest for every admissible k.

items.value: Zero such primes exist
items.reasoning: The digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 sum to 15, which is divisible by 3, and rearranging digits never changes the digit sum. So every five-digit number formed from these digits is divisible by 3 and is far larger than 3 itself, hence composite. Enumerating all 120 permutations confirms that none is prime.

items.value: The symbol stands for the digit 3
items.reasoning: Writing the digit as d, the five addends are d, 10 + d, 50 + d, 11d and 10d + 1, summing to 24d + 61, while the right-hand side 1dd equals 100 + 11d. Setting 24d + 61 = 100 + 11d gives 13d = 39, so d = 3. Substituting back: 3 + 13 + 53 + 33 + 31 = 133, which is indeed of the form 1dd with d = 3.

items.value: 0.25 foot
items.reasoning: Laying the sticks end to end and measuring differences lets you obtain any whole-number combination of 7.5 and 3.25 feet, and the smallest positive length so obtainable is their highest common measure. In hundredths of a foot that is the HCF of 750 and 325, which is 25, i.e. 0.25 foot. A construction: 7.5 - 2(3.25) = 1 foot and 3(3.25) - 7.5 = 2.25 feet, and 2.25 - 2(1) = 0.25 foot. No smaller length, in particular 0.05 foot, is reachable, since every combination is a multiple of 0.25.

The operation is 'subtract 1': 14, 18, 20, 24, 30 and 32 become 13, 17, 19, 23, 29 and 31, which are consecutive prime numbers. The next prime after 31 is 37, so the next term of the given sequence is 37 + 1 = 38. Of the alternatives, 34, 36 and 40 would need 33, 35 and 39 to be prime, and none is.

items.value: The torn page carried the numbers 7 and 8
items.reasoning: A torn leaf removes two consecutive page numbers, an odd followed by its even successor, so the original total 1 + 2 + ... + n must equal 195 plus that pair's sum. The four option pairs sum to 11, 15, 19 and 23, giving candidate totals 206, 210, 214 and 218, and only 210 is a triangular number - it is 20 x 21 / 2, so the booklet had 20 pages. 210 - 195 = 15, which is 7 + 8, and 7 with 8 is a valid leaf. No other option produces a whole number of pages.

items.value: The blanks are filled by a, c, c and e, giving abababcbcbcdcdcdeded
items.reasoning: Read the arrangement as ten two-letter blocks. The second letter of each block is already fixed and runs b, b, b, b, b, d, d, d, d, d. Filling the blanks with a, c, c, e makes the first letters run a, a, a, c, c, c, c, c, e, e - the only one of the four options that never goes backwards through the alphabet - and makes the whole string ab ab ab / cb cb / cd cd cd / ed ed, a clean 3-2-3-2 structure in which each step advances exactly one of the two letters. Options A, B and D all produce a doubled block such as bb or dd and a first-letter sequence that runs d before c, which no reading of the pattern supports. Marked MED because a pattern item of this kind is settled by which reading is most regular rather than by proof.

items.value: The difference between A and D is 3
items.reasoning: With every letter a distinct digit greater than 3, the units column C + F must end in 2 and the tens column B + 2 must end in 0, forcing B = 7 with a carry, which in turn fixes E = 5 from the hundreds column 3 + E + carry ending in 9. That leaves A + D = 15 with both digits above 3 and distinct from 5 and 7, so {A, D} = {6, 9}. An exhaustive search over all digits 4 to 9 returns exactly four solutions - 6374 + 9528, 6378 + 9524, 9374 + 6528 and 9378 + 6524 - and every one of them gives |A - D| = 3.

items.value: Even taken together the two statements cannot settle whether the book has more than 100 figures
items.reasoning: S1 caps the count at 2 x 51 = 102 but allows anything down to zero, so alone it cannot decide. S2 puts a floor of 51 but no ceiling, so alone it cannot decide either. Together they confine the total to the range 51 to 102, and that range straddles 100 - the book could have 60 figures (answer no) or 102 (answer yes). Since the two statements together still admit both answers, C is correct and A is wrong.

The English averages fix the ratio of girls to boys: (9g + 8b)/(g + b) = 8.8 gives 9g + 8b = 8.8g + 8.8b, so 0.2g = 0.8b and g = 4b. Applying that same 4:1 ratio to Hindi, x = (8 x 4b + 7 x b)/(5b) = 39/5 = 7.8. The result is independent of the actual class size, as checking b = 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 confirms.

items.value: R is S's wife
items.reasoning: Q is female (a mother-in-law) and U is female (P's daughter); T and S are male, so exactly one of P and R is male. If P were female, R would be male and his wife would have to be U or P - but Q, not P, would then be U's mother, and making P his wife would put Q a generation above P and give three generations. So P is male and R is female. R's husband is then S (T is unmarried, and P is U's father), making Q the mother of S; the second couple must therefore be P and Q, whose children are S, U and T. That leaves T and U as the two unmarried siblings, and the tally is three males (P, S, T) and three females (Q, U, R) across two generations. R is female, so A is impossible; S is married to R, so C is false.

items.value: In a leap year 12th July is a Sunday
items.reasoning: From 12 January to 12 July is 19 + 28or29 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 12 days, that is 181 days in an ordinary year and 182 in a leap year. In a leap year 182 is exactly 26 weeks, so 12 July falls on the same weekday as 12 January - a Sunday - which makes C true and D false. In an ordinary year the gap of 181 days leaves a remainder of 6, so 12 July is a Saturday. 15 July is three days later than 12 July in either case, giving Wednesday in a leap year and Tuesday otherwise, so A and B are both false.

items.value: Assumptions 1, 3 and 5 are valid
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 follows from the passage's core claim that FDI is volatile across time, sectors and regions and that the responsibility for employment cannot be left to it. Assumption 5 follows from the closing point that technology diffusion may fail because India's physical and human capital is inadequate - human capital being built by public spending on education and health. Assumption 2 is refuted by the passage itself, which calls FDI's volatility 'a necessary consequence of their search for the highest returns', i.e. inherent rather than policy-curable, and assumption 4 asserts a priority of public over private investment that the passage never draws. That eliminates A and C. Assumption 3 is the judgement call - the passage notes that foreign private investment is more volatile than private investment in general, which points to domestic private investment as the steadier alternative - but D ('3 only') is untenable because 1 and 5 are clearly supported, so B is the only coherent option.

items.value: Only implications 1 and 2 - inter-linking of rivers and a network of dams and canals
items.reasoning: The passage identifies two problems: monsoon flows are concentrated in four months (a seasonal problem, answered by 'holding rainwater in reservoirs for subsequently releasing it', which is implication 2) and are spatially skewed while river water runs unused into the sea (answered by inter-linking, implication 1). The other three have no basis in the text: borewells concern groundwater, which the passage never discusses; legal regulation of agricultural water use is not mentioned; and nothing is said about the Union Government or about who should allocate river water between regions. Every option other than A contains at least one of those three, so A is the only defensible choice.

items.value: Only assumption 3 is valid - economic freedom has a positive impact on building human capital
items.reasoning: The passage's central claim is that the return on education rises with the level of economic freedom and that people invest in education when free to enjoy its benefits, which is assumption 3 - education being the building of human capital. Assumption 2 reverses the passage's causality: it makes education produce economic freedom, whereas the passage makes economic freedom produce investment in education. Assumption 1 overstates with the word 'invariably' and narrows to 'higher education'; the passage argues that lower tax rates create an incentive to invest in education, not that they always and necessarily result in it.

items.value: Urban local bodies must recover costs through user charges
items.reasoning: The passage says sustainable water delivery is impossible 'unless financing mechanisms are put in place', lists the heavy costs involved, and closes with the decisive point that water could be delivered free only if cities were rich enough to meet the entire cost - 'They are not.' The message is therefore that the cost has to be recovered from users. B blames efficiency, which the passage never discusses; its argument is entirely about money. C is defeatist in a way the passage is not, and D introduces a cap on city populations that is nowhere in the text.

items.value: Only assumption 2 is valid - sustainable water delivery means much more than supplying water to households
items.reasoning: The passage lists collection from a natural source, treatment, a distribution network, sewerage infrastructure and sewage treatment plants as all part of sustainable delivery, so it plainly assumes the task extends well beyond piping water to homes - assumption 2. Assumption 1 misreads the closing sentences: the passage says that if cities were rich enough water could be delivered free, not that only rich cities can deliver it sustainably. Its whole point is the opposite - that cities which are not rich can still manage it, provided financing mechanisms are in place.
